title: Nitrogen in Plants: What It Does and When Your Crop Needs It
metaTitle: Nitrogen in Plants: Role, Signs and When to Apply
metaDescription: Nitrogen in plants builds every leaf and protein. See what it does, when palay, mais and gulay need it most, and how to keep it from going to waste.
excerpt: Nitrogen in plants is the nutrient of green growth. It is built into chlorophyll, the green color that turns sunlight into food, and into every protein and enzyme, so a crop short of it stays small and pale. Palay, mais and leafy vegetables take more of it than any other nutrient. Here is what it does, when each crop needs it most, and how to keep it from going to waste.

blocks.text:
Every leaf a plant makes is built partly from nitrogen. It sits at the heart of the amino acids that make up proteins, and proteins run the whole plant: they build new cells, drive growth and form the enzymes that carry out the chemistry of life. Nitrogen is also part of chlorophyll, so the deep green of a well fed field is nitrogen you can see.

That is why nitrogen sets the size of the plant and the size of the harvest. In palay it decides how many tillers form and how many of them carry a panicle. In mais it sets the length of the ear and the number of kernels. For pechay and cabbage it is most of what you sell, because the harvest is the leaves themselves.
A building block, used up as the crop grows

Nitrogen is a building block, not a helper. A helper nutrient such as zinc switches on an enzyme and works again and again in tiny amounts. Nitrogen instead becomes part of the plant body, in every protein and every leaf, so the crop uses it up as it grows and the harvest carries it out of the field.

A crop of palay takes away roughly 15 to 20 kilograms of nitrogen for every ton of grain, counting the straw. So the soil alone rarely holds enough for a full harvest, and nitrogen has to come back every season, from fertilizer, manure, compost or a legume grown before.

Nitrogen moves freely inside the plant. When the roots cannot find enough, the plant pulls it out of its oldest leaves and sends it to the young ones. So the lower leaves yellow first, often from the tip back, while the top stays green for a while.

That is the sign to watch for: yellowing that climbs from the bottom up, on a plant that also stays short and thin. See [nitrogen deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/nitrogen-deficiency) for how it looks in each crop, and what else can look like it.
When nitrogen in plants is most critical

Nitrogen is needed the whole season, but a few stages decide the yield. In palay the tillers are counted early and the grains per panicle are set at panicle initiation, so those are the windows to feed. In mais the plant takes most of its nitrogen in the weeks of fast growth before tasselling.

DAT means days after transplanting, DAS days after sowing in the field, and DAP days after planting. The days are the usual ones for a typical variety, so a long or short variety moves them a little. Timing nitrogen in plants to these windows gets more harvest from the same bags. Our guide to [fertilizer timing by growth stage](/blog/fertilizer-timing-by-growth-stage) puts them together for a whole season.

Here is when it matters most for each crop, from the same stage book the anee.io calendar reads:

items: Palay, transplanted: Nitrogen after flowering is barely used. It feeds blast, sheath blight and hoppers and risks lodging.
Yellow corn: Nitrogen after early grain fill rarely pays. The ear draws on what the leaves hold.
Sweet corn: Nitrogen near the milk stage is wasted and can lower ear quality.
Leafy vegetables (pechay, cabbage): Nitrogen near harvest raises leaf nitrate and makes heads loose and soft.
Fruit vegetables (tomato, eggplant, pepper): Heavy nitrogen at flowering grows leaves instead of fruit and invites pests.
Gourds and melons (ampalaya, squash): Heavy nitrogen at flowering makes vines leafy and fruit set poor.
Legumes (mungbean, peanut, sitaw): Nitrogen after nodules form shuts down fixing and is mostly wasted.
Root crops (kamote, cassava): Nitrogen after roots begin swelling grows tops at the cost of roots.
Onion and garlic: Nitrogen after bulbing starts gives thick necks and bulbs that rot in storage.
Sugarcane: Nitrogen after grand growth keeps cane growing and lowers sugar at harvest.
Banana: Nitrogen near harvest only feeds the follower sucker, not the bunch.
Other grains (sorghum): Nitrogen after flowering is barely used and invites lodging and disease.

blocks.text: What keeps nitrogen from the crop

Nitrogen is easy to lose. Urea left on the surface of wet soil turns to ammonia gas within days, and in a flooded paddy part of it escapes as gas when the water stands too long. Heavy rain and typhoons also wash nitrate below the roots, most of all on sandy soil.

So split the dose instead of giving it all at once: a little at planting, more when the crop starts its fastest growth, and the rest before the stage that sets the harvest. Work urea into the soil, or broadcast it into shallow water and keep the water in, so more of it stays for the crop. Soils low in organic matter hold little nitrogen of their own, so they need the split doses most.

Most farms here buy nitrogen as urea, the cheapest nitrogen per kilogram. The other common fertilizers add a second nutrient with it, so pick by what the soil also lacks. See our guide to [urea fertilizer](/blog/urea-fertilizer) for rates and timing, and the [rice fertilizer schedule](/blog/rice-fertilizer-schedule) for palay.

items: Urea (46 0 0): the most nitrogen per bag, for topdressing.
Ammonium sulfate (21 0 0): nitrogen with sulfur, good on alkaline soil.
Ammonium phosphate (16 20 0) and complete fertilizer (14 14 14): nitrogen with phosphorus at planting.
Chicken manure, compost and a legume grown before: slower nitrogen that also feeds the soil.

blocks.title: Too much nitrogen is a problem too
blocks.text: Too much nitrogen makes soft, dark green leaves that blast, sheath blight and planthoppers love, and tall weak stems that lodge in the first strong wind. In palay it also delays heading. Give what the crop needs at each stage, not more.

blocks.title: See if your nitrogen lasts to the stages that need it
blocks.text: Put your fertilizers on your crop's calendar in anee.io and the [Coverage Planner](/features/residual-effect-calendar) shows, day by day, whether nitrogen reaches the stages that need it, and where it runs out. Free to start.

items.q: Is nitrogen a macronutrient or a micronutrient?
items.a: Nitrogen is a primary macronutrient, along with phosphorus and potassium. Crops take it in tens of kilograms per hectare, far more than any micronutrient.

items.q: When should I apply nitrogen to palay?
items.a: Split it. Give a small part as basal, the biggest share at active tillering, and the last dose at panicle initiation, about 35 to 45 days after transplanting for most varieties. Nitrogen after flowering is barely used.

items.q: Why do the lower leaves turn yellow first?
items.a: Because nitrogen moves inside the plant. A hungry plant takes it from its old leaves to feed the new ones, so the oldest leaves yellow while the top stays green.

items.q: Can I give nitrogen through the leaves?
items.a: Yes, a weak urea spray can green up vegetables quickly. But leaves take up only small amounts at a time, so most of the season's nitrogen still has to go to the soil.
